# Peugeot 206: Dash and Clock Backlights Failed After Head Unit Reinstall

A common pattern in automotive electronics is a symptom that appears only after a module swap or reinstallation. In your case, the dashboard and clock backlights ceased functioning immediately after you adjusted the wiring on the head unit and reassembled the dash. This temporal correlation strongly suggests that the issue isn't a random fuse failure, but rather an electrical load mismatch or a short circuit introduced during the adjustment process.

The fact that you have already verified the fuses in both the battery panel and the under-steering-wheel box is excellent troubleshooting hygiene. However, in this specific architecture, the head unit often acts as a voltage reference for the instrument cluster's illumination circuit rather than just a power consumer. When you "adjusted wires," you likely altered the resistance of the path or inadvertently bridged two lines that shouldn't be connected. If the backlight circuit relies on the head unit's internal logic to ground the illumination signal, disconnecting or shorting a pin during adjustment can create an open circuit or a direct short to ground that blows a fuse instantly upon reconnection.

Consider the power flow here. The head unit typically receives constant battery voltage (B+) and switched ignition voltage (ACC). The instrument cluster usually shares this ACC line for its backlight control. If you touched the wiring harness near the connector without isolating the pins, you might have created a momentary short that caused the fuse to blow. You mentioned checking fuses, but if the fuse blew while the dash was connected and you didn't notice the "pop" or smell of burning because the cluster loads are low, it could be an intermittent short that only manifests when the full load is applied after reassembly.

To diagnose this without fully disassembling the dash again, isolate the head unit. Disconnect the harness connector from the back of the head unit while the ignition is in the ON position. Observe if the dashboard lights return. If they do, the fault lies within the head unit itself or the specific pins you touched. If the lights remain off with the head unit disconnected, the issue is in the wiring harness between the battery/fuse box and the instrument cluster, likely a fuse that blew during your initial adjustment but wasn't visible until now, or a broken wire in the ground path for the cluster.

If the lights return when the head unit is unplugged, you must inspect the specific pins involved in the illumination signal. Many Peugeot 206 models use a dedicated pin on the head unit harness that switches ground to activate the backlight. If you adjusted wires and accidentally bent this pin or created a short between it and a constant 12V line, the fuse will blow every time you reconnect. Check for a faint arc mark or discoloration around the connector housing where the pins meet.

Another possibility is that the head unit's internal power supply rail, which drives the backlight output, was damaged during the adjustment. If the head unit has an internal short on its illumination output pin, connecting it back will immediately draw excessive current, blowing the fuse again or causing a voltage drop that prevents the cluster from lighting up even if the fuse is replaced. In this scenario, replacing the head unit or repairing the specific board section is necessary.

Before tearing apart the entire dashboard, use a multimeter to check the continuity of the ground wire leading to the instrument cluster with the head unit disconnected. If the ground path is open, you have a broken wire inside the dash harness that likely got severed during reassembly. If the resistance is near zero but no light occurs, check for voltage at the input side of the fuse feeding the cluster illumination. If voltage is present there but not at the cluster connector, the issue is definitively in the head unit or its connection to the cluster.

This approach minimizes unnecessary disassembly while systematically isolating whether the fault is in the power distribution (fuses/wires) or the module (head unit). By understanding that the head unit often controls the ground side of the backlight circuit, you can pinpoint why a simple wire adjustment caused a total failure of the illumination system.
